title: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya  - Carbon Brief
gist: COP31 in Antalya ended nearly 50 hours late with the 'Antalya pact' cover decision rejected, agriculture talks collapsing (derailed partly by CBAM disputes), and few hard outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature. Article 6 carbon-market rules stayed light-touch despite integrity flaws, adaptation finance targets were dropped, and forest/ocean finance pledges (e.g. TFFF at $8.2bn vs a $10bn target) fell short.

insights.claim: The COP31 'Antalya pact' cover decision, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected by at least 32 countries including the EU and UK in the closing plenary, after the summit ran nearly 50 hours over time.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Multilateral climate process is producing weaker binding signals; policy-driven climate trades should lean on national/regional policy rather than UNFCCC outcomes.
insights.locator: Cover decision

insights.claim: Parties failed to agree the COP31 cover text chiefly because all references to fossil fuels had been removed and it lacked concrete climate-finance targets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: No new UN-level fossil-fuel phase-out language — removes a headline regulatory overhang for oil & gas from this cycle.
insights.locator: Ultimately, parties did not find consensus

insights.claim: The rejected COP31 cover decision 'welcomed' carbon dioxide removal (including tree planting) immediately after recognising forests and oceans as greenhouse-gas sinks, worrying experts about offsetting via nature.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals rising political acceptance of CDR in UN texts — supportive for CDR developers if the language resurfaces at COP32.
insights.locator: Experts, however, were concerned

insights.claim: No draft of the COP31 cover decision mentioned the COP17 biodiversity summit or the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, reflecting 'toxic' politics over climate-nature synergies.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Climate and biodiversity policy tracks remain siloed; nature-finance products tied to GBF get little UNFCCC tailwind.
insights.locator: None of the iterations of the rejected cover decision

insights.claim: Food-systems advocates argued that language in COP cover decisions rarely translates into on-the-ground impact, making negotiation tracks a more effective lever than cover-text references.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Discount headline COP cover-text wording when assessing real policy impact on agriculture.
insights.quote: What we often find is that getting references or language to things in the cover decision doesn’t really play out as impacts on the ground
insights.locator: However, observers told Carbon Brief

insights.claim: UNFCCC agriculture negotiations (Sharm el-Sheikh joint work on agriculture) collapsed for the second year running at COP31, ending with only a procedural text punting substance to Bonn and COP32 in Ethiopia.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: No multilateral agriculture-emissions framework is imminent; ag-sector climate regulation remains national.
insights.locator: Agriculture and food security

insights.claim: The Arab group derailed COP31 agriculture talks by arguing fertilisers are vital to food security and that fertiliser exports are being hurt by the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), demanding trade measures be discussed.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: CBAM is biting on fertiliser exporters enough to be weaponised in negotiations — watch fertiliser trade flows and CBAM exposure of Gulf/North African producers.
insights.locator: However, in the first negotiating session

insights.claim: Observers said the underlying blocker in COP31 agriculture talks was not bad faith but developed countries' failure to deliver climate finance, leaving nothing in the negotiation for global-south countries.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Finance shortfalls are the binding constraint on multilateral climate deals across tracks.
insights.quote: The main issue is not bad-faith negotiating; it’s the fact that, across the UNFCCC, the countries that have a climate debt are not paying it
insights.locator: Marie Cosquer, advocacy analyst

insights.claim: A fundamental rift persists over whether UNFCCC agriculture work should focus on adaptation only (India, G77 and China) or also pursue mitigation co-benefits (EU and others).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Mitigation mandates on farming emissions (e.g. fertiliser, livestock) face structural opposition from large emerging markets.
insights.locator: At the same time, said Camp

insights.claim: Technical expert reviews of 16 national Article 6.2 carbon-trading reports found 543 inconsistencies, 115 of them significant, and no report was free of issues.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Integrity risk in sovereign bilateral carbon credits is material — price in reputational/reversal risk for ITMO buyers.
insights.locator: Across 16 national reports checked so far

insights.claim: COP31 dropped draft language flagging Article 6.2 integrity problems with concern; the final decision merely 'takes note', leaving the bilateral carbon-trading 'wild west' untightened.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Light-touch Article 6.2 regime persists — favourable for deal volume (e.g. Singapore-Peru), negative for credit-quality assurance.
insights.locator: However, this entire paragraph disappeared

insights.claim: IETA and the Project Developer Forum lobbied for a 'course correction' arguing Article 6.4 market rules are too conservative and failing to attract investment in carbon projects.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Industry pressure to loosen Paris carbon market rules is real; supply growth in 6.4 credits depends on outcome of 2028 rules review.
insights.quote: current version of [the market] is failing to attract investment in carbon projects
insights.locator: On Article 6.4, negotiations began

insights.claim: After EU pushback, the final COP31 Article 6.4 text dropped a requested formal assessment of the 'cumulative impact' of conservative rules, only asking the supervisory body to consider how standards operate together, with a full rules review starting in 2028.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: No near-term loosening of 6.4 crediting standards; the 2028 review is the next catalyst for carbon-credit supply.
insights.locator: However, after pushback from the EU

insights.claim: Singapore is positioning itself as a hub for Article 6 carbon markets, announcing bilateral Article 6.2 projects with Peru at COP31, and the Antalya statement endorsing carbon markets reached 17 signatories after Colombia, Ghana and Peru joined.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Singapore is the jurisdiction to watch for compliance-grade carbon-credit trading volume in Asia.
insights.locator: Singapore, in particular, wanted

insights.claim: Guyana declared jurisdictional forest carbon markets its 'principal pathway', but Carbon Market Watch called it very problematic, citing an investigation where a single spreadsheet error produced 3.9m excess credits.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional forest credits carry quantification risk; buyers of large sovereign forest-credit issuances face integrity exposure.
insights.locator: At the forest leaders’ summit on 11 November

insights.claim: 45 scientists signed a COP31 open letter warning that Article 6 rules let temporary carbon storage in forests and soils be credited against fossil-fuel emissions that affect the climate for thousands of years.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Permanence critique of nature-based credits is gaining scientific weight — durable CDR may command a growing premium.
insights.quote: They allow temporary carbon storage in forests, soils and other ecosystems to be credited against fossil-fuel emissions that will affect the climate for thousands of years.
insights.locator: Towards the end of the summit, 45 scientists

insights.claim: Efforts to define tripling adaptation finance as $120bn by 2035 failed at COP31; developed countries wanted it inside the broader $300bn climate-finance goal so it could come from many sources.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: No ring-fenced adaptation-finance number — public flows for adaptation infrastructure remain uncertain.
insights.locator: Finance dominated the negotiations on adaptation

insights.claim: COP31 resolved the adaptation fund's transition to serve the Paris Agreement by giving each UN region board seats, unlocking its access to 5% of Article 6.4 carbon-market revenues.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Links Paris carbon-market activity directly to adaptation funding — growth in 6.4 issuance now funds adaptation.
insights.locator: Other adaptation items included the transition

insights.claim: Agreement on the just transition mechanism (Belem-Antalya Mechanism) was deferred, with a phased approach aiming for adoption at COP32 in Ethiopia in November 2027.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: COP32 is the next decision point for just-transition finance architecture.
insights.locator: Late on 21 November, an unbracketed text

insights.claim: The COP31 just transition text referenced critical minerals in a COP decision for the first time, but parties removed human-rights due diligence across critical-mineral supply chains.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Critical minerals entering UNFCCC texts without due-diligence obligations — lower near-term compliance burden for miners, but a marker of rising scrutiny.
insights.locator: Additionally, critical minerals were referenced

insights.claim: COP31's just transition work programme explicitly endorsed agroecological farming approaches, a first that food-systems advocates hailed as a landmark.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gives policy legitimacy to agroecology, a mild headwind narrative for input-intensive agriculture (fertilisers, agrochemicals).
insights.locator: Food-systems advocates were, however, heartened

insights.claim: A first COP31 draft called on developed countries to phase out unilateral trade-restrictive measures, such as the EU CBAM and deforestation law, by end-2027, but all trade references were cut and none survived the conference.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: CBAM and EUDR survive untouched by UNFCCC pressure — EU border carbon pricing continues on schedule.
insights.locator: Trade and climate featured strongly

insights.claim: Russia, Brazil, Kenya, the Arab and African groups protested the treatment of trade at COP31, with Kenya and Ghana signalling unilateral trade measures will be a priority at COP32.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Expect escalating CBAM confrontation at COP32 in Ethiopia; trade-climate friction is a growing geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: climate policy should not turn into trade policy by other means
insights.locator: Russia’s representative remarked

insights.claim: The EU, UK and Canada blocked the COP31 response-measures decision, arguing it would unduly influence the next global stocktake via cross-border impact assessments on inflation, trade flows and debt.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Developed countries are resisting formal accounting of spillover costs of their climate policies on developing economies.
insights.locator: During the final plenary, the EU

insights.claim: Negotiations on synergies between the climate, biodiversity and desertification Rio conventions were blocked from the first hour, with Russia and the Arab group opposing discussion and ending in a one-line text.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Integrated climate-nature policy is stalled multilaterally.
insights.locator: Climate and nature ‘synergies’

insights.claim: COP31 failed to be the promised 'blue COP': ocean text with 19 mentions died with the rejected pact, leaving only voluntary items like the Antalya ocean and seas compact without targets or finance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Blue-economy investors should not expect UN-mandated ocean finance flows near term.
insights.locator: In the end, oceans had 19 mentions

insights.claim: WRI analysis found 95% of coastal and island countries include ocean-based action in their national climate plans, but over 60% of ocean-commitment implementation depends on external support.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Ocean climate action is finance-constrained — a demand pool for blended blue finance.
insights.locator: Analysis published by the World Resources Institute

insights.claim: New ocean pledges at COP31 were small: a UK £20m marine-protection package and an Australian $10m Blue Pacific commitment.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Scant public ocean money confirms limited near-term sovereign funding.
insights.locator: Also on the ocean thematic day

insights.claim: The Tropical Forest Forever Facility has mobilised $8.2bn, mostly as conditional loans, leaving it $1.8bn short of its $10bn 2026 target, after COP31 produced only $88m in new philanthropic pledges plus Canada's up-to-$393m.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: TFFF capitalisation is lagging — key forest-finance vehicle at risk of under-delivery.
insights.locator: This means the fund has – so far – mobilised $8.2bn

insights.claim: Norway's up-to-$3bn loan to the TFFF is conditional on the fund reaching $10bn by end-2026, creating a cliff risk unless the deadline is extended.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Watch whether the $10bn deadline is extended; failure could unwind Norway's anchor commitment.
insights.locator: Norway’s “up to $3bn” loan

insights.claim: A political economist warned the TFFF will be unable to deliver the promised $4 per hectare of protected forest even in a best case, due to less capital and fewer risks taken.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Payment-for-forest-protection economics may disappoint tropical forest nations.
insights.locator: Political economist Max Alexander Matthey

themes.theme: Methane, food subsidies, biofuels and lobbying

insights.claim: $480m in new private funding was pledged at COP31 for methane and other super pollutants, with methane framed as the 'emergency brake' after confirmation of an inevitable 1.5C overshoot.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Methane abatement (monitoring, leak detection, landfill, livestock) is gaining priority as near-term warming lever.
insights.quote: cutting its emissions is our emergency brake to slow warming
insights.locator: Chief of the UN Environment Programme

insights.claim: Only nine of the 159 Global Methane Pledge countries reaffirmed the 30%-by-2030 methane cut at COP31, and Australia's farm lobby welcomed that its government imposed no methane obligations on farmers.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Agricultural methane regulation remains politically resisted in major beef exporters.
insights.locator: Nine of the 159 countries

insights.claim: Governments spend roughly $840bn a year on agricultural support and subsidies, which a Clim-Eat report argues should be redirected to soil health, infrastructure and targeted farm incomes.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Subsidy reform is a large latent policy lever for agri-input and agri-food markets.
insights.locator: This noted that governments spend approximately $840bn

insights.claim: The COP31 venue was powered by 3m litres of biodiesel despite Turkey championing electrification, with cited research claiming biodiesel can be 80% worse for the climate than fossil fuels due to land-use change.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Biofuel climate credentials remain contested — regulatory risk for crop-based biodiesel.
insights.locator: In the first week of the summit, Devex

insights.claim: The India-led Global Biofuels Alliance added Papua New Guinea and is co-launching a roadmap to protect domestic carriers against international aviation carbon levies.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Biofuel blocs are organising against aviation carbon levies — relevant to SAF and airline cost outlook.
insights.locator: On 6 November, the India-led Global Biofuels Alliance

insights.claim: DeSmog found 260 food-and-agriculture lobbyists at COP31 (down from 302 at COP30), but fertiliser lobbyists rose 45%, and a record 700 carbon capture and storage lobbyists attended per CIEL.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Rising fertiliser and CCS lobbying presence signals these industries see high policy stakes in the UN process.
insights.locator: DeSmog analysis found 260 lobbyists

insights.claim: Observers warned the proliferation of voluntary COP action-agenda initiatives should not be confused with progress, as negotiated outcomes diverge from on-the-ground action.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Discount announcement counts; track national policy and investment changes instead.
insights.quote: we should be careful not to confuse the growing number of initiatives with progress
insights.locator: Maryam Rezaei, food-systems lead at ODI
